Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on I1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question. Patrick Flynn's FamilySearch person ID is not recorded in the project tree; the router should locate the FamilySearch profile for I1 (Patrick Flynn, b. ~1845 Ireland, d. 1908 Schuylkill County PA) to retrieve hints.

Patrick Flynn's 1908 death certificate (project source S3, cert. no. 4521) is already obtained and sourced on the tree death fact, but its parentage fields have not been extracted for this question. Pennsylvania death certificates from 1906 forward include informant-supplied fields for father's name and mother's maiden name. Reviewing this image first could directly name Thomas Flynn as father and supply the mother's name, answering both halves of the parentage question at minimal cost. This is also the dedicated death-entry item required because Patrick's birth parish in Ireland is unknown, making a baptism search impossible without first narrowing the origin. The tree records Patrick's birthplace as Ireland (sourced from the 1850 census) while the project objective states Pennsylvania — the death certificate birthplace field should be noted to resolve this starting-point discrepancy (BCG Standard 11). Locality entry loc_001 confirms Pennsylvania civil death registration began 1906, so this certificate exists.

The United States Census, 1880 (FamilySearch collection 1417683) is name-searchable. The 1880 schedule is the first US census to explicitly record each person's relationship to the head of household; a listing of Patrick (b. ~1845, age ~35) in Thomas Flynn's (b. ~1818, age ~62) Schuylkill County household as 'son' would be the strongest census evidence of the father-son relationship yet found. Existing census evidence (S1 1850, S2 1860) is co-residence inferred from household position and shared surname, not a stated relationship. If Thomas's wife appears in the household, her given name advances the mother-identification question. Search Schuylkill County with spelling variants Flynn, Flinn, Flyn.

The United States Census, 1870 (FamilySearch collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Patrick (~age 25) and Thomas (~age 52) were likely still in Schuylkill County. The 1870 schedule does not state relationships explicitly but household composition corroborates the co-residence pattern and may show the wife's given name for the first time. This item is a fallback for the 1880 census (pli_003) — if Patrick is not found in 1880, the 1870 entry fills the gap and keeps the household evidence chain intact across the period from S2 (1860) to the 1880 and later censuses. Search Schuylkill County with spelling variants Flynn, Flinn, Flyn.

The United States Census, 1900 (FamilySearch collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Patrick (b. ~1845) would be ~55. The 1900 schedule asks for father's birthplace and mother's birthplace separately for each person, and records year of immigration and years in the US — columns that can narrow the family's Irish county of origin. Thomas (b. ~1818) would be ~82 if alive; more likely deceased by 1900, but his widow (Patrick's mother, if she survived) may appear in a related household. Search Schuylkill County for Patrick Flynn and any widow of Thomas Flynn, with spelling variants.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) was alive in the 1860 census (tree source S2) and could have died any time from ~1860 to ~1900 — the plausible death window sized to Thomas's lifespan as the record creator, not limited to Patrick's research window. Schuylkill County probate records (Register of Wills, available from 1811 per locality entry loc_001) are a primary parentage source: a will naming 'my son Patrick Flynn' is direct evidence of the father-son relationship and would likely name the widow as administratrix, supplying her given name and advancing the mother question. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); the county volumes also appear as FamilySearch image group 007936749 (Probate Records 1851-1930), also browse-only. Project source S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is listed in the tree but carries no assertions for q_001, indicating Thomas Flynn's probate has not yet been searched. Browse image-by-image through the docket index for 'Flynn' with spelling variants.

If Thomas Flynn's probate (pli_006) yields no record or names no wife, Schuylkill County deed records are the fallback. Pennsylvania law required a wife's signature (relinquishment of dower rights) on land conveyances, so deeds signed by Thomas Flynn would typically bear his wife's name as co-grantor — supplying the mother's first name at minimum. FamilySearch volume 007936752 (Deed Records 1815-1900) is 22% record-searchable; the remainder requires image browse. Search for grantor 'Thomas Flynn' with spelling variants and examine each deed for the wife's co-signature.

Dedicated parentage-question item for the parents' marriage record. A marriage record for Thomas Flynn and his wife (a) confirms the couple as a married unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census records do not include; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) corroborates Thomas as father when the current evidence is indirect household co-residence. Thomas (b. ~1818) and wife likely married before ~1845, either in Ireland before immigration or in Schuylkill County after arrival. The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable and covers 1708-1985 — search for Thomas Flynn as groom with spelling variants. FamilySearch volume 007936753 (Marriage Records 1870-1910, browse-only (personCount 0)) covers civil records as a supplementary browse if the church search is inconclusive. Note the mother's surname from this record may be a prior married name rather than her birth name if she was previously widowed; pli_009 (sibling baptisms) pairs with this to test that possibility.

Required FAN item for a parentage question. Patrick's siblings' baptism records in Schuylkill County would name both parents in each entry — father Thomas and mother including her maiden name — making this FAN evidence about Patrick's parentage rather than an independent research goal for the siblings. The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable — search for children of Thomas Flynn to surface siblings; each entry names both parents. FamilySearch volume 007936751 (Church Records 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0) as a supplementary image browse. If different entries give the mother different surnames across time, she may have remarried between children — each surname variant warrants its own follow-up under pli_008. Locality entry loc_001 notes Schuylkill County Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are held at the parish and diocese, not the county.

Naturalization records for Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) could name his specific county of origin in Ireland — information needed if the parents' marriage or Patrick's baptism must ultimately be traced in Irish church records. FamilySearch volume 007936750 (Naturalization Records 1849-1915) covers Schuylkill County and is browse-only (personCount 0). Pre-1906 first-paper declarations and petitions often recorded the applicant's place of birth; some Pennsylvania counties' records also named a wife. Thomas would have naturalized in the 1850s-1870s. Browse image-by-image for 'Flynn' with variants. If this locates the Irish county of origin, a follow-on plan for Irish diocese baptism records (for Patrick b. ~1845) would be warranted. This item is a fallback for pli_008 (parents' marriage) — if the PA church marriage search cannot be located and the Irish origin is unknown, naturalization may supply the missing geographic anchor.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

Continued occupation as miner in Schuylkill County would corroborate the family tradition. The 1890 census was largely destroyed and is not available. Search variant spellings.

FAN item: Sibling Patrick Sheahan (I2) purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 — seven years before Michael's documented arrival — documented by deed S1 (Deed Book 42 p. 118). Patrick's established presence as a landowner, not merely a transient laborer, is the strongest candidate explanation for why Michael moved to Schuylkill County specifically rather than another coal county. Also search the United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable, personCount above 0) for Patrick's household and occupation to confirm he was employed in mining by the time Michael arrived.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable (personCount above 0). Roman Catholic parishes in the anthracite coal region specifically served Irish immigrant communities; a sacramental record naming Michael Sheahan in a Schuylkill County parish would corroborate the 1882 arrival date and may name an origin parish. The locality entry also notes that Catholic parishes here fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875), with sacramental registers held at the parish and diocese level. These are contextual derivative sources that can corroborate or refute the coal-mining family tradition and name the specific mine or employer. Relevant titles are held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County in Pottsville, Pennsylvania; digitized newspaper collections may be available via Chronicling America. Search as a fallback if Pennsylvania State Archives mine inspection records are not accessible or do not cover the relevant collieries.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US federal census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) falls two years before Michael's recorded 1882 Schuylkill arrival. A search will show whether he was living in Schuylkill County by June 1880 (move already made) or still elsewhere in Pennsylvania (move imminent), and will record his occupation, household composition, and state and country of birth. This is the highest-priority record because it places Michael precisely in the transition period. The tree records his residence as Pennsylvania in 1870 (F1, from S1) and Schuylkill County in 1882 (F2, from S1); the 1880 census spans that gap. Variant spellings to try: Sheehan, Shahan, Shehan.

The 1900 US federal census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) is the first federal census to ask foreign-born respondents for their year of immigration and number of years in the United States. An entry for Michael Sheahan in Schuylkill County in 1900 would confirm his continued presence in the coal region, record his occupation eighteen years after arrival, and — if born outside the US — state his immigration year and country of birth. That immigration year establishes whether his 1882 Schuylkill arrival coincided with his first entry into the country (transatlantic migration for mining work) or followed an earlier US arrival (an internal Pennsylvania move). Variant spellings to try: Sheehan, Shahan, Shehan.

Patrick Sheahan (I2), Michael's brother, is documented in Schuylkill County by the 1875 deed record (S2), seven years before Michael's 1882 arrival. Chain migration drove most labor movement into the anthracite coal region: earlier arrivals secured jobs and lodging for those who followed through kinship networks. The 1880 census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) for Patrick in Schuylkill County would show his occupation, the borough or township where he lived, and his household — establishing the employment network and specific locale Michael most likely joined. If Patrick's 1880 record names a colliery or mining borough, that concentrates the search for mine employment records (item 7). This FAN item bears directly on the question: Patrick's prior establishment in the coal region is the strongest explanation for why Michael chose Schuylkill County specifically.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (1708–1985) is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Pennsylvania did not begin civil birth and death registration until 1906, so sacramental registers are the primary route to pre-1906 events. The anthracite coal region's Irish Catholic community was served by parishes under the Diocese of Philadelphia (elevated to archdiocese in 1875); the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, covers the northern Pennsylvania counties but not Schuylkill — so records search within the Philadelphia archdiocesan orbit. An entry for Michael Sheahan in a Schuylkill County Catholic register from the 1880s or 1890s could record his place of origin, his date of arrival at the parish, or — in a burial or marriage entry — his age and birthplace. Variant spellings to try: Sheehan, Shahan, Shehan.

The Schuylkill County naturalization records volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0) on FamilySearch. Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization record the applicant's country and place of birth, the date and port of US arrival, and the current county of residence — information that would directly establish whether Michael's 1882 Schuylkill arrival was his first entry into the United States or a domestic move from elsewhere in Pennsylvania. This item is a fallback for item 2 (the 1900 census): if the census yields no result or does not clearly supply the immigration year, the naturalization file provides that data from Michael's own sworn declaration.

The Schuylkill County deed records volume (image group 007936752, 1815–1900) is partially searchable on FamilySearch (22% of images are indexed). The locality guide (loc_001) notes that coal-region laborers frequently leased rather than purchased land from mining companies, so the absence of a deed does not disprove residence; a purchase would, however, confirm an intention to settle permanently. Michael's brother Patrick is documented buying land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (S2, Deed Book 42, p. 118); Michael may appear in the same or adjacent books as buyer, grantor, or boundary witness. A deed would also name the specific borough or township, concentrating the church and mine-record searches.

Mine payrolls, company ledgers, and mine inspection reports are the most direct potential evidence that Michael Sheahan was employed at a named colliery in Schuylkill County after 1882, and they are the record type that would most concretely confirm the family tradition of mining-work as the motive for the move. No tool result this session returned a digitized mine-records collection for Schuylkill County; holdings vary by company and survive unevenly. This item requires verifying availability with the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Schuylkill County Historical Society before it can be searched. If items 3 or 6 identify the specific mining borough where Patrick and Michael settled, that would concentrate the colliery search to a narrower set of company records.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Tree facts already recorded bearing on this question:**
- I1 (Patrick Flynn): Birth ~1845, Ireland (sourced to 1850 census, S1); Death 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, PA (sourced to death cert no. 4521, S3). No spouse or children in tree.
- I2 (Thomas Flynn): Birth ~1818, Ireland. No death date or place recorded. No sources directly attached to I2.
- Relationship R1 (ParentChild, I2 → I1): cited from S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census), S3 (death cert); all at quality 2.
- Proof summary ps_001 is at tier "probable" and explicitly names the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses and Thomas Flynn's probate as the primary remaining gaps.
- Source description S4 ("Schuylkill County Probate Records, Schuylkill County Register of Wills") is already in the tree but no assertions have been extracted from it.

**Plan pl_003 — 7 items:**

- **pli_006** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch, no fallback — Patrick (~25) likely still in county; Thomas (~52) may be in the same household. 1870 does not have the relationship column, so co-residence is indirect evidence. "United States Census, 1870" is name-searchable. Search Flynn variants (Flin, Flinn, Flyne).
- **pli_007** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch, no fallback — first census year to record relationship to head of household; Thomas listed as "father" would be direct parentage evidence, the single most diagnostic item in this plan. "United States Census, 1880" is name-searchable.
- **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch, no fallback — Patrick was alive in June 1900 (died March 1908); 1900 records birth month/year and years in the US, corroborating the ~1845 birth and Irish origin. Thomas's presence or absence narrows the probate date window. "United States Census, 1900" is name-searchable. (1890 census was largely destroyed; not planned.)
- **pli_009** — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1870–1910, Schuylkill County Register of Wills — Thomas Flynn's will naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and could alone advance ps_001 to proved. Date window set to Thomas's plausible lifespan (b. ~1818, could have died roughly 1870–1910), not Patrick's window. S4 already identifies this repository; no assertions yet extracted. Added for breadth (BCG Standard 14).
- **pli_010** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, Ancestry — fallback for pli_006; independently compiled index at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/
- **pli_011** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, Ancestry — fallback for pli_007; at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/6742/; especially important given 1880's relationship column
- **pli_012** — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, Ancestry — fallback for pli_008; at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7884/

**Fallback relationships:** pli_010 → pli_006; pli_011 → pli_007; pli_012 → pli_008. Probate (pli_009) is a co-equal primary, not a fallback.

**Total scope:** 7 searches (4 primaries, 3 fallbacks only triggered if the corresponding primary yields nothing).

Hand-back: search-records for pli_006, pli_007, pli_008, and pli_009 (all FamilySearch or a county repository reachable via FamilySearch catalog); search-external-sites for pli_010, pli_011, pli_012 (Ancestry).

---

This plan picks up exactly where the prior research left off. The three federal censuses from 1870, 1880, and 1900 are searched in chronological order on FamilySearch — all three are fully indexed, so Patrick Flynn can be looked up by name. The most important year is 1880, because that is the first census to record how each person in a household relates to the head, meaning Thomas Flynn appearing there as "father" would be the clearest statement yet that he is Patrick's parent. Alongside the censuses, the plan adds a search of Schuylkill County probate records for a will from Thomas Flynn, since a will naming Patrick as a son would be direct proof of parentage on its own. Ancestry fallbacks are lined up for each census year in case the FamilySearch index misses an entry. If any of the FamilySearch searches come back empty, the Ancestry version of that year is tried next.

The census searches on FamilySearch will be executed next, starting with the 1870 record for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

However, no assertions for q_001 have been extracted from S3; the only two q_001 assertions (a_004, a_005) came from the 1850 census. The 1908 certificate was issued under Pennsylvania civil death registration, which began in 1906 (locality guide loc_001); it exists and is the highest-probability source for direct identification of both parents. The informant may have named the mother as well as the father, and the certificate form asks for each parent's birthplace. This collection is name-searchable.

The 1880 census is the first U.S. census to record each person's relationship to the household head, making it the most valuable census year for identifying Thomas Flynn's wife — Patrick's candidate mother. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) would be approximately 62 in 1880; if alive, his household would list his wife by name and explicit relationship. Patrick (born ~1845) would be ~35 and may appear as a son or in a neighboring household. The proof summary (ps_001) confirms post-1860 censuses have not yet been searched for q_001; the 1860 census (tree source S2) is the last census attached to relationship R1. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. Variant spellings Flynn and Flinn should be tried.

The 1870 census bridges the gap between the 1860 household (tree source S2, Thomas and Patrick co-residing) and the critical 1880 household (pli_002). Thomas Flynn (~52 in 1870) and Patrick Flynn (~25) may still be co-residing; any woman in the household at that census would be a candidate for Thomas's wife and Patrick's mother. The United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable.

Patrick Flynn, born ~1845 and dying 1908-03-12, was alive for the 1900 census (approximately age 55). The 1900 census asks for each person's parents' birthplaces, which would confirm both parents were born in Ireland. If Patrick was married, the household entry would supply his wife's name and the years married. The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable.

The project tree already lists S4 ('Schuylkill County Probate Records') as a source description but it is not attached to any assertion or relationship for q_001 — it has not been mined for parentage data. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) last appears in the 1860 census (tree source S2); a will or letters of administration in Schuylkill County naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of the father–son relationship, which currently rests only on census co-enumeration. A will may also name Thomas's wife, identifying Patrick's mother. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); the Schuylkill County probate image volume (image group 007936749, 1851–1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0). The date window runs to 1910 because Thomas, born ~1818, could plausibly have lived into his late eighties; the window is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required for a parentage question. The couple's marriage record would: (a) confirm Thomas and his wife as a unit; (b) supply the mother's maiden name, which census records omit; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborate Thomas as father where parentage currently rests on census co-enumeration alone. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable and covers 1708–1985; an Irish Catholic marriage is the most likely form in this community (loc_001 notes RC parishes in Schuylkill were under the Diocese of Philadelphia). Note the limit: the marriage record proves the couple wed — it does not establish that Patrick is their child; that requires a record placing Patrick with both parents. Because no mother's surname is yet known, the search runs on Thomas Flynn's name alone. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn should be tried.

Loc_001 notes that RC parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. A browse may also surface baptism records for Patrick or his siblings naming Thomas and his wife together.

FAN-cluster item required for a parentage question. Under Pennsylvania law, when a husband conveyed real property, his wife's dower interest required her separate acknowledgment in the deed — a dower release naming her by given name and married surname. A deed in Thomas Flynn's name in Schuylkill County may therefore record his wife's given name directly, establishing Patrick's mother. The Schuylkill County Deed Records volume (image group 007936752, 1815–1900) is 22% name-searchable. The deed's boundary recital also names adjoining landowners who are likely FAN members from the same Irish-origin community; their own church, probate or land records may further corroborate the family unit. What this reveals about Patrick: his mother's given name (from the dower release) and probable kin or neighbours who could corroborate the household.

Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 in Ireland, would have filed a declaration of intention and a petition for naturalization, most likely in Schuylkill County where he resided by 1850. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). An early declaration may give Thomas's Irish county of origin, his wife's name, and his date of arrival — information that narrows the search for Irish parish records (where a baptism for Patrick would be found if born before emigrating) and may identify the mother's name. The date window runs to ~1898 because Thomas, born ~1818, could plausibly have lived into his late eighties; the window is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

---

**Mode:** Create — Plan `pl_001`

**Known baseline facts:**
- Born c. 1814, Kentucky
- Last confirmed alive: 1870 census, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky (age ~56)

**Important context:** Kentucky did not issue statewide death certificates until 1 January 1911. Since Elijah was born c. 1814 and last seen alive in 1870, his death almost certainly predates 1911. The plan searches pre-1911 county death registers (the nearest equivalent) first, and uses probate records as the primary corroborating source.

---

**8-item research plan (in execution order):**

| # | Type | Target | Repository | Notes |
|---|------|--------|------------|-------|
| pli_001 | Vital record | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1910 | FamilySearch | Collection 1804888 "Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970" — name-searchable; try variant "Wilkens" |
| pli_002 | Vital record (browse) | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1852–1910 | FamilySearch | Browse-only images, volume 007991103; only ~4% indexed — page through year-by-year after 1870 if pli_001 is a nil |
| pli_003 | Vital record | Kentucky, 1911–1935 | FamilySearch | Collection 1417491 — statewide certificates; rules out any late death (age ~97+) |
| pli_004 | Census | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1880 | FamilySearch | Determines whether Elijah was alive on 1 June 1880; narrows the death window |
| pli_005 | Probate (browse) | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1895 | FamilySearch | Volume 007834412, administrator bonds & estate settlements — filed within days of death |
| pli_006 | Court (browse) | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1895 | FamilySearch | Volume 007834430, Court Order Books — letters of administration cross-reference the death |
| pli_007 | Vital record | Kentucky, 1870–1910 | Ancestry | "Kentucky, U.S., Death Records, 1852–1965" — fallback if FamilySearch index misses the entry |
| pli_008 | Cemetery | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1920 | FindAGrave | Headstone dates approximate death date and localize to a township |

---

**Next steps:** Execute pli_001 first (name-searchable on FamilySearch → `search-records`), followed by the 1880 census (pli_004). If the name index misses Elijah, browse the unindexed images (pli_002). Probate (pli_005–006) is the most reliable source for a pre-1911 Kentucky death.

County death registers (Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970, collection 1804888) exist for 1852-1910 but 1860s-1870s coverage is partial; many counties have no surviving register for those decades.

For a death before 1911, the primary evidence is probate: administrator bonds (naming the widow or adult son), estate settlements, and probate register entries bracket the death date within months and localize it to the county.
Muhlenberg County probate records survive well for the 1870s and are in Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) — browse-only images organized by county and volume.
Church burial registers and cemetery records can also bracket the death.

Browsing the unindexed pages for the years immediately after 1870 — when Elijah was last confirmed alive — may surface his death entry even when the index misses it. Search 'Wilkins' and 'Wilkens' in any indexed portion first, then browse year by year.

A person born c. 1814 would have been approximately 97 in 1911 — unlikely but not impossible. A quick name search on 'Wilkins' and 'Wilkens' restricted to Muhlenberg County for 1911-1935 will confirm or rule out a late death that would carry a formal statewide certificate. The 1870 residence fact in the tree (fact F2) establishes he was alive at 56, leaving a plausible but narrow window for living past 1911.

Browsing the 1870-1895 pages may surface an order naming Elijah and either corroborate or refine a death date found in item 5, or supply one where the probate volume is silent. The date range matches the lifespan window set in item 5.

Search 'Wilkins' and 'Wilkens' scoped to Muhlenberg County for 1870-1910 as a second-repository check after items 1-2.

Find a Grave holds memorials for Muhlenberg County cemeteries that often record death dates drawn from headstone inscriptions or burial registers. A burial entry for Elijah Wilkins (or Wilkens) would supply a date that approximates the actual death date and, if a cemetery name is given, locates the death to a specific township or community within Muhlenberg County. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.
